units.translation: where in M the first hand has written above the line ὀχυροῖσι [strong, secure]; but ἐχυροῖς [strong, secure] 88 ἐχυροῖς ἕρκεσιν εἴργειν ἄμαχον κύμα θαλάσσας [to ward off with strong barriers the irresistible wave of the sea], where several copies have ὀχυροῖς [strong, secure], which is read at Ag. 44 ὀχυρὸν ζεῦγος Ατρείδαιν [the strong pair of the Atreidae], unless this too should be written ἐχυρόν [strong, secure]. In the same way the manuscripts of other writers vary, as the examples collected in the Thesaurus show.

strong, secure

to have, hold

(with imperfect εἶχον [I had], whose third person dual is είχέτην [they two had] at Ch. 760, aorist ἔσχον [I had], future ἕξω [I will have] or, more rarely, σχήσω [I will have]) corresponds to Latin habeo, but not infrequently also to other verbs, in all of which, however, the notion of having is present. It is used not only of things that can be held or touched with the hands, but also of things that are perceived by sight, hearing, or mind. Examples of common usage collected by Wellauer are these, some of which will have to be discussed under the words compounded with ἔχειν [to have].
Of the place which someone occupies
I hold occupied
By inverted construction, a place or condition is said to hold someone
ἔχω [I have] I restrain
ἔχω [I have] constructed with an infinitive means I can, I have the power, I know how
Without an infinitive
ἔχω [I have] with a participle
Of the same kind is ἔχω [I have] followed by an interrogative pronoun in formulas
ἔχω [I have] used intransitively of one who is in some place or condition
Most often it is joined with adverbs indicating state or condition
in a verse not read in M, but invented by a Byzantine interpolator
thus Salmasius for ἔχων [having]
by tmesis said for οὖς ἀνέχων [holding up the ears], i.e. ἄνω ἔχων [holding up], as the grammarians indicated in the annotation explain.
about which see Thes. vol. 3 p. 2618.
where it is sustineat.
unless ἡστ᾽ [he was sitting] should be written.
ἐφημένου [sitting upon] Burges, rightly Wieseler corrected to ἔχων – ἐφεζόμην [having – I was sitting upon].
Butler for ἀμηχάνως ἐμοί [helplessly to me].
For you two the command of Zeus holds its fulfillment
has nets around his limbs
surely still of me – the ruler of the blessed will have need
the son of Cronus has a heart that cannot be soothed

but of the wretched mortals he took no account
creatures of a day, having blazing fire
whoever keeps his foot outside of troubles

what way of life each of them has

has a worthy practice
